morningSummary:
Tuesday, 17 November 2026 — Night News & Global Update. Updated at 20:00 Europe/Paris. Presented by Sophie Laurent.

TOP DEVELOPMENTS — Simon Ekpa has reportedly been released from custody in Finland, according to lawyer Aloy Ejimakor and reporting by Punch Newspapers and Anadolu Agency. The release does not overturn his terrorism-related conviction: Finland's Court of Appeal upheld the conviction in October and reduced his sentence from six years to four. The precise legal basis of today's release, including whether it is parole or another form of conditional release, remains to be confirmed.

NIGERIA — The ADC has filed an appeal and asked the Court of Appeal to restrain INEC from changing its leadership records and candidate details while the legal challenge is pending. The appeal is not itself a stay order. The 5 November judgment affecting the David Mark-led leadership and Atiku's nomination remains under challenge. Separately, consultations involving Atiku Abubakar, Peter Obi and Seyi Makinde have not produced a publicly confirmed common ticket or coalition programme. Nigeria's annual inflation eased to 14.06% in October, but food inflation remained 19.13% and household costs remain high. Defence Minister Christopher Musa says US intelligence sharing and satellite support are helping operations against militants and bandits; those operational claims should be distinguished from independently verified outcomes.

MIDDLE EAST — The Gulf remains tense. Reports describe a merchant-vessel incident near the Strait of Hormuz, while the United States has expanded its naval presence to three carrier groups. Iran launched drones at a US military radar facility in Bahrain; Bahrain says its air defences intercepted them without reported casualties or damage. The risk to shipping, energy infrastructure and regional diplomacy remains elevated.

EUROPE — EU foreign ministers accused Russia of prolonging Ukraine peace talks while attacks threaten power and heating infrastructure ahead of winter. The EU announced new sanctions targeting nearly 50 Russian banks and financial institutions and other individuals and businesses. France experienced a nationwide public-sector strike over pay and purchasing power. Separately, five European countries announced plans for a small migrant return hub in Rwanda; France is not participating, and human-rights and legal questions remain.

AFRICA — Ethiopia expelled six Sudanese consular staff and ordered the Sudanese consulate in Assosa closed as tensions between the two countries deepen. Sudan and Ethiopia accuse each other of supporting armed groups; both deny the allegations, which AP says it could not independently verify. In East Africa, a Dangote-linked investment vehicle reportedly acquired nearly 25% of Kenya Pipeline Company, a development with potential implications for regional fuel distribution.

ASIA-PACIFIC — Japan protested after two suspected Russian military aircraft reportedly entered Japanese airspace near Fukuoka. Tokyo scrambled fighters and lodged a formal protest. At APEC, Canada and China announced further targeted tariff concessions after Mark Carney met Xi Jinping. The proposed Trump-Xi-Putin trilateral meeting in Shenzhen remains a planned diplomatic event; no outcome should be reported before it takes place.

GLOBAL ECONOMY AND PUBLIC INTEREST — Oil and shipping markets remain sensitive to Gulf security risks. Trade concessions between Canada and China may ease selected barriers but are not a comprehensive trade agreement. Across all regions, RadiantWaves distinguishes confirmed events from official claims, allegations, proposals and pending legal proceedings.

topStories.title: ADC files appeal and asks Court of Appeal to restrain INEC over Atiku and other nominations
topStories.summary: The ADC has asked the Court of Appeal to overturn the 5 November judgment affecting the David Mark-led leadership and to restrain INEC from changing party leadership records or candidate details while the appeal is pending. The appeal is not itself proof that a stay has been granted.
topStories.content: The African Democratic Congress has taken its challenge to the Court of Appeal, asking it to overturn the Federal High Court judgment of 5 November that nullified the David Mark-led party leadership and affected decisions taken under that structure. Daily Post reported on Tuesday that the party is also seeking an order restraining the Independent National Electoral Commission from altering its leadership records or candidate nomination details while the appeal is determined. The ADC argues that the trial court acted on an amended process that was already under appeal and that immediate implementation could make a successful appeal ineffective. The case began with a challenge by former deputy national chairman Nafiu Bala Gombe. INEC previously said it would study the certified judgment and obtain legal advice before deciding what action to take. The key distinction remains that filing an appeal does not automatically suspend a judgment; the court must determine any application for interim protection or stay. No final appellate decision or confirmed stay order was established in the reporting reviewed for this edition.

topStories.title: Atiku, Obi and Makinde consultations continue, but no opposition coalition agreement has emerged
topStories.summary: Seyi Makinde has confirmed consultations with Atiku Abubakar and Peter Obi on political cooperation. No common ticket, coalition programme or final agreement has been announced, while other opposition groups are promoting different arrangements.
topStories.content: Discussions among opposition figures remain active as Nigeria approaches the 2027 general election. Oyo State Governor Seyi Makinde has confirmed consultations involving former Vice-President Atiku Abubakar and Peter Obi, but Premium Times reported on 16 November that negotiators had not announced a common ticket or shared policy programme. The Nigeria Democratic Congress has separately advocated support for an Obi-Kwankwaso ticket. These developments should not be merged into a single confirmed coalition. Political consultations, endorsements, party mergers and formal changes to nominations are distinct processes governed by party rules and electoral law. The ADC's leadership litigation adds another layer of uncertainty for Atiku's political position. For voters, the substantive questions include how any proposed alliance would select candidates, settle internal disputes, publish a policy platform and ensure accountability after an election.

topStories.title: Nigeria's annual inflation eases to 14.06%, but households still face high food costs
topStories.summary: Nigeria's annual headline inflation eased to 14.06% in October from 14.63% in September. Annual food inflation also slowed to 19.13%, but prices remain high and month-on-month inflation data show that easing annual inflation does not mean the cost of living has fallen.
topStories.content: Nigeria's annual headline inflation rate eased to 14.06% in October from 14.63% in September, according to data reported by Reuters from the National Bureau of Statistics. Annual food inflation fell to 19.13% from 19.59%. The figures provide evidence that the pace of annual price increases has moderated, but they do not mean that prices have returned to earlier levels. Many households continue to face elevated costs for food, transport, energy and essential services. President Bola Tinubu's administration has defended reforms including the removal of petrol subsidies and currency devaluation as necessary to strengthen public finances and support longer-term growth. Critics point to the immediate burden on consumers and businesses. The political debate ahead of the 2027 election will increasingly focus on whether slower inflation translates into real improvements in purchasing power, employment and household welfare.

topStories.title: Nigeria says US intelligence support is helping operations against militants and bandit networks
topStories.summary: Defence Minister Christopher Musa says US intelligence sharing, satellite imagery and training are supporting Nigerian operations against militant and bandit groups. The minister also cited expected helicopter deliveries and expanded regional cooperation.
topStories.content: Nigeria's Defence Minister Christopher Musa said US intelligence sharing, satellite imagery and training are helping Nigerian forces conduct frequent operations against armed groups in the north-west and north-east. Reuters reported that Musa described overnight operations that killed several militant leaders and said Nigeria expected additional helicopters from the United States and Italy. Security cooperation is taking place amid the long-running insurgency involving Boko Haram and Islamic State West Africa Province, widespread banditry and kidnappings. Nigeria is also working with Cameroon, Niger and Chad on cross-border operations and efforts to disrupt financing and logistics. The minister warned that Islamic State Sahel was seeking links with criminal gangs in the north-west. These are official statements and operational claims; independent verification of each reported casualty or tactical result is not always available. The wider test is whether improved intelligence and equipment lead to sustained civilian protection, fewer kidnappings and safe access to schools, farms and markets.

topStories.content: Maritime security risks remain elevated around the Strait of Hormuz. Reports on Tuesday described a tanker or merchant-vessel incident near Oman's coast, while the UK Maritime Trade Operations centre has issued warnings about attacks and suspicious activity in the wider region. The United States has expanded its naval presence to three aircraft-carrier groups as the confrontation with Iran continues. Iran has threatened shipping and has accused Washington of escalating pressure through a naval blockade. The Gulf remains a vital route for oil and liquefied natural gas exports, meaning disruption can affect freight costs, insurance premiums, energy prices and supply chains well beyond the Middle East. Details about individual incidents, including the identity of attackers and the precise weapons used, should be treated as unconfirmed unless established by maritime authorities. Bahrain said its air defences intercepted the attack and that there were no reports of casualties or damage. Tehran has described its actions as retaliation for US attacks and surveillance, while Washington says it is monitoring threats and has not reported damage from this incident. The confrontation is unfolding alongside a US naval blockade affecting Iranian oil exports and stalled diplomatic contacts. Regional governments including Egypt, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates have condemned Iranian attacks, while Qatar has warned that further escalation could undermine diplomacy. The risk is that military incidents, maritime threats and economic pressure become mutually reinforcing. topStories.title: EU accuses Russia of prolonging Ukraine talks while attacks threaten winter power supplies
topStories.summary: EU foreign ministers say Russia is dragging out peace talks while attacking Ukrainian energy infrastructure ahead of winter. The EU has imposed new sanctions on nearly 50 Russian banks and financial institutions and other targets.
topStories.content: European Union foreign ministers accused Russia of prolonging negotiations over Ukraine while continuing attacks on power plants and other infrastructure as winter approaches. The EU announced sanctions affecting nearly 50 Russian banks and financial institutions, energy- and oil-linked businesspeople, and individuals accused of spreading pro-Russian disinformation. EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said there was no ceasefire and that attacks continued to weaken Ukraine. Moscow has promoted a different European security framework, which EU ministers rejected. US-led talks have not produced a lasting ceasefire, with territorial control and future security guarantees among the central disputes. European governments say future discussions should include senior security advisers from France, Germany, the United Kingdom, Italy and Poland alongside EU officials. The immediate humanitarian concern is the effect of strikes on heating, electricity and water systems as temperatures fall.

topStories.title: Japan protests after suspected Russian aircraft enter its airspace near Fukuoka
topStories.summary: Japan says two suspected Russian military aircraft crossed into its airspace near Fukuoka for about five minutes on Tuesday. Tokyo scrambled fighter jets and lodged a formal protest with Moscow.
topStories.content: Japan said two suspected Russian military aircraft violated its airspace near Fukuoka in south-western Japan for approximately five minutes early on Tuesday. The Japanese military scrambled fighter aircraft and issued warnings. Defence Minister Shinjiro Koizumi described the incident as a serious threat to sovereignty and safety, and said Tokyo had lodged a strong protest demanding measures to prevent a repeat. The aircraft reportedly crossed the Tsushima Strait and continued south towards waters between Taiwan and Yonaguni. Taiwan also reported tracking two Russian aircraft in its air-defence identification zone, while South Korea said Russian aircraft entered its identification zone without violating South Korean airspace. The incidents come amid strained Japan-Russia relations and concern about increased Russian-Chinese military activity in the region. Air-defence identification zones are not identical to sovereign airspace; each claim must be described precisely.

topStories.title: Five European countries plan migrant return hub in Rwanda; rights and legal questions remain
topStories.country: Germany / Austria / Denmark / Greece / Netherlands / Rwanda
topStories.summary: Germany, Austria, Denmark, Greece and the Netherlands have announced plans for a small-scale return hub in Rwanda for some rejected asylum seekers who cannot or will not return home. The proposed centre could host about 100 people; France is not participating.
topStories.content: Five European governments — Germany, Austria, Denmark, Greece and the Netherlands — have announced plans to establish a small-scale migrant return hub in Rwanda. The proposed facility is intended for adults whose asylum applications have been rejected and who cannot or will not return to their countries of origin. The plan envisages capacity of around 100 people and says residents could receive temporary permits, integration support, education, health care and employment assistance, with the possibility of seeking voluntary return home. Negotiations are expected to continue into early 2027, with operations later that year if the project proceeds. France has declined to participate. Supporters say the scheme could improve the effectiveness of returns; critics question whether a centre of this scale can meaningfully address a much larger European returns system and warn about human-rights safeguards and legal challenges. The announcement is a plan, not evidence that the centre is already operating.

topStories.title: France faces nationwide public-sector strike over pay and purchasing power
topStories.summary: Public-sector unions staged a nationwide strike on 17 November, demanding better pay, jobs and public-service funding. Disruption was reported in several cities as the government faces pressure over purchasing power.
topStories.content: France experienced a new day of public-sector industrial action on Tuesday, with unions calling for higher wages, more jobs and stronger public services. The action involved workers across public administration and education, with demonstrations and disruption reported in several cities. The dispute follows tensions between Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu's government and unions over the postponement of negotiations on public-sector purchasing power. Union representatives say workers are facing rising living costs and deteriorating working conditions. The government has argued that wage and budget decisions must be considered within wider fiscal constraints. The scale of disruption varies by region and service, and travellers should consult local transport operators for current information. The strike is also part of a broader political debate over public spending, wages and the government's ability to build compromise.

topStories.title: Sudan-Ethiopia tensions deepen after consular expulsions and mutual accusations
topStories.summary: Ethiopia has expelled six Sudanese consular staff and ordered Sudan's consulate in Assosa closed. The move follows Sudanese allegations that Ethiopia allowed RSF-linked forces to use its territory; Ethiopia and the UAE deny supporting the RSF.
topStories.content: Relations between Sudan and Ethiopia have deteriorated further after Ethiopia expelled six Sudanese consular staff and ordered Sudan's consulate in the western city of Assosa to close. The action follows Sudan's accusations that drones used by the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces to attack infrastructure were supplied by the United Arab Emirates and launched from Ethiopian territory. Sudan has filed complaints with the United Nations Security Council and African Union. Ethiopia and the UAE deny supporting the RSF. Ethiopia has in turn accused Sudan of supporting rebels in its Tigray region. The Associated Press says it could not independently verify the competing allegations. The dispute is especially concerning because Sudan's war has already caused mass displacement and severe humanitarian needs, while tensions in Ethiopia's border regions remain unresolved. Diplomatic expulsions reduce channels for communication at a time when regional de-escalation is needed.

topStories.title: Canada and China signal further tariff concessions after Carney-Xi meeting
topStories.summary: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney says Canada and China have agreed further targeted tariff reductions following his meeting with Xi Jinping. The reported measures cover selected Canadian pork and seafood exports and Chinese steel and aluminium products.
topStories.content: Canada and China have agreed to expand selected tariff concessions following talks between Prime Minister Mark Carney and President Xi Jinping during the APEC meetings. The arrangement is reported to include reduced Chinese tariffs on some Canadian pork and seafood exports, while Canada extends tariff-remission measures for selected Chinese steel and aluminium products. The targeted concessions are intended to ease trade friction and support market access, but they do not amount to a comprehensive free-trade agreement. The talks are taking place as Canada seeks to diversify export markets while managing its security and economic relationship with the United States. Canadian exporters will be watching the detailed implementation rules, product coverage and timing. Businesses should not assume that every tariff has been removed or that all sectors have been included.

topStories.whatHappensNext: Watch for official tariff schedules, implementation dates and the response from affected Canadian and Chinese industries.

topStories.title: Africa's energy and logistics investment: Dangote-linked firm secures Kenya Pipeline stake
topStories.summary: A Dangote investment vehicle acquired nearly 25% of Kenya Pipeline Company for about $327 million, according to AfricaTells. The stake could give the company a board nomination and has implications for regional fuel distribution.
topStories.content: An investment vehicle linked to Nigerian industrialist Aliko Dangote has acquired nearly a quarter of Kenya Pipeline Company, according to AfricaTells' 17 November regional briefing. The reported purchase was valued at approximately $327 million and makes the investor the second-largest shareholder after the Kenyan government. Kenya Pipeline operates a network carrying petroleum products from Mombasa inland and to neighbouring markets including Uganda, Rwanda, South Sudan and the Democratic Republic of Congo. The investment may give the shareholder the right to nominate a director to the company's board. The development is relevant to regional fuel supply and Dangote's broader ambitions in refining and distribution. The commercial implications will depend on governance arrangements, regulatory oversight, pipeline access terms and the progress of any planned refinery projects. The investment should not be interpreted as evidence that a new refinery is already operational.

Defence Minister Shinjiro Koizumi described the incident as a serious threat to sovereignty and safety, and said Tokyo had lodged a strong protest demanding measures to prevent a repeat. The aircraft reportedly crossed the Tsushima Strait and continued south towards waters between Taiwan and Yonaguni. Taiwan also reported tracking two Russian aircraft in its air-defence identification zone, while South Korea said Russian aircraft entered its identification zone without violating South Korean airspace. worldNews.content: Five European governments — Germany, Austria, Denmark, Greece and the Netherlands — have announced plans to establish a small-scale migrant return hub in Rwanda. The proposed facility is intended for adults whose asylum applications have been rejected and who cannot or will not return to their countries of origin. The plan envisages capacity of around 100 people and says residents could receive temporary permits, integration support, education, health care and employment assistance, with the possibility of seeking voluntary return home. articles.title: Simon Ekpa reported released from Finnish custody; conviction remains in force
articles.category: Nigeria / Finland / Security / Rule of Law
articles.summary: Nigerian and international outlets report that Simon Ekpa was released from custody in Finland on 17 November. Lawyer Aloy Ejimakor said he received confirmation from Ekpa's associate David Matsanga, and Anadolu Agency reported a video said to show Ekpa leaving prison. The legal basis of the release, including whether it is conditional release or parole, has not been independently established in the reporting reviewed.
articles.content: Simon Ekpa, the Nigerian-born separatist figure convicted in Finland on terrorism-related offences, was reported released from custody on Tuesday. Punch Newspapers said lawyer Aloy Ejimakor confirmed the development after speaking with Ekpa's close associate David Matsanga. Anadolu Agency also reported the release and described a video shared by Ngozi Orabueze showing Ekpa emerging from prison. Ekpa was arrested in November 2024 and convicted in September 2025. In October 2026, Finland's Court of Appeal upheld the conviction while reducing the sentence from six years to four. The release therefore must not be described as an acquittal or reversal of the conviction. Punch said it could not confirm whether the release was parole. The precise legal mechanism, any supervision requirements and any restrictions should be confirmed through Finnish authorities or court records. The case has implications for security and public debate in south-eastern Nigeria, where violence associated with separatist armed groups has affected civilians, businesses and public services. Claims about individual responsibility for particular attacks must continue to be assessed against evidence and court findings.

articles.imageNote: Regional illustration; not a photograph of Ekpa or the reported release.
articles.source: Punch Newspapers; Anadolu Agency; Africa Check background fact-check

articles.whatHappensNext: Seek confirmation from Finnish prison or court authorities on the legal basis, conditions and any remaining sentence obligations.

articles.title: ADC files appeal and asks Court of Appeal to restrain INEC over Atiku and other nominations
articles.summary: The ADC has asked the Court of Appeal to overturn the 5 November judgment affecting the David Mark-led leadership and to restrain INEC from changing party leadership records or candidate details while the appeal is pending. The appeal is not itself proof that a stay has been granted.
articles.content: The African Democratic Congress has taken its challenge to the Court of Appeal, asking it to overturn the Federal High Court judgment of 5 November that nullified the David Mark-led party leadership and affected decisions taken under that structure. Daily Post reported on Tuesday that the party is also seeking an order restraining the Independent National Electoral Commission from altering its leadership records or candidate nomination details while the appeal is determined. The ADC argues that the trial court acted on an amended process that was already under appeal and that immediate implementation could make a successful appeal ineffective. The case began with a challenge by former deputy national chairman Nafiu Bala Gombe. INEC previously said it would study the certified judgment and obtain legal advice before deciding what action to take. The key distinction remains that filing an appeal does not automatically suspend a judgment; the court must determine any application for interim protection or stay. No final appellate decision or confirmed stay order was established in the reporting reviewed for this edition.

articles.title: Atiku, Obi and Makinde consultations continue, but no opposition coalition agreement has emerged
articles.summary: Seyi Makinde has confirmed consultations with Atiku Abubakar and Peter Obi on political cooperation. No common ticket, coalition programme or final agreement has been announced, while other opposition groups are promoting different arrangements.
articles.content: Discussions among opposition figures remain active as Nigeria approaches the 2027 general election. Oyo State Governor Seyi Makinde has confirmed consultations involving former Vice-President Atiku Abubakar and Peter Obi, but Premium Times reported on 16 November that negotiators had not announced a common ticket or shared policy programme. The Nigeria Democratic Congress has separately advocated support for an Obi-Kwankwaso ticket. These developments should not be merged into a single confirmed coalition. Political consultations, endorsements, party mergers and formal changes to nominations are distinct processes governed by party rules and electoral law. The ADC's leadership litigation adds another layer of uncertainty for Atiku's political position. For voters, the substantive questions include how any proposed alliance would select candidates, settle internal disputes, publish a policy platform and ensure accountability after an election.

articles.whyItMatters: Opposition coordination may shape the choices available to voters, but credibility depends on transparent procedures and a coherent public programme.
articles.whatHappensNext: Look for published coalition terms, party decisions, candidate filings and INEC updates.

articles.title: Nigeria's annual inflation eases to 14.06%, but households still face high food costs
articles.summary: Nigeria's annual headline inflation eased to 14.06% in October from 14.63% in September. Annual food inflation also slowed to 19.13%, but prices remain high and month-on-month inflation data show that easing annual inflation does not mean the cost of living has fallen.
articles.content: Nigeria's annual headline inflation rate eased to 14.06% in October from 14.63% in September, according to data reported by Reuters from the National Bureau of Statistics. Annual food inflation fell to 19.13% from 19.59%. The figures provide evidence that the pace of annual price increases has moderated, but they do not mean that prices have returned to earlier levels. Many households continue to face elevated costs for food, transport, energy and essential services. President Bola Tinubu's administration has defended reforms including the removal of petrol subsidies and currency devaluation as necessary to strengthen public finances and support longer-term growth. Critics point to the immediate burden on consumers and businesses. The political debate ahead of the 2027 election will increasingly focus on whether slower inflation translates into real improvements in purchasing power, employment and household welfare.

articles.background: The NBS publishes headline and food inflation measures. Annual inflation compares prices with the same month a year earlier; it is not a measure of whether the overall price level has returned to normal.
articles.whyItMatters: The cost of living remains a central test of economic policy and a major issue for households, employers and political parties.
articles.whatHappensNext: Watch subsequent NBS releases, food supply, transport costs, exchange-rate movements and whether wage growth catches up with prices.

articles.title: Nigeria says US intelligence support is helping operations against militants and bandit networks
articles.summary: Defence Minister Christopher Musa says US intelligence sharing, satellite imagery and training are supporting Nigerian operations against militant and bandit groups. The minister also cited expected helicopter deliveries and expanded regional cooperation.
articles.content: Nigeria's Defence Minister Christopher Musa said US intelligence sharing, satellite imagery and training are helping Nigerian forces conduct frequent operations against armed groups in the north-west and north-east. Reuters reported that Musa described overnight operations that killed several militant leaders and said Nigeria expected additional helicopters from the United States and Italy. Security cooperation is taking place amid the long-running insurgency involving Boko Haram and Islamic State West Africa Province, widespread banditry and kidnappings. Nigeria is also working with Cameroon, Niger and Chad on cross-border operations and efforts to disrupt financing and logistics. The minister warned that Islamic State Sahel was seeking links with criminal gangs in the north-west. These are official statements and operational claims; independent verification of each reported casualty or tactical result is not always available. The wider test is whether improved intelligence and equipment lead to sustained civilian protection, fewer kidnappings and safe access to schools, farms and markets.

articles.background: Nigeria faces a multi-front security challenge involving insurgency, banditry, kidnappings and cross-border armed networks.
articles.whyItMatters: Security cooperation matters only if it improves protection for civilians and accountability as well as operational capacity.
articles.whatHappensNext: Watch for independently confirmed operational outcomes, equipment deliveries, civilian protection measures and regional coordination.

articles.title: Tanker incident near Hormuz and US naval build-up heighten Gulf shipping risks
articles.summary: A merchant vessel was reportedly attacked north of Khasab, Oman, while the United States has expanded its naval presence in the region to three carrier groups. The incident adds to tensions over Iran, shipping security and the Strait of Hormuz.
articles.content: Maritime security risks remain elevated around the Strait of Hormuz. Reports on Tuesday described a tanker or merchant-vessel incident near Oman's coast, while the UK Maritime Trade Operations centre has issued warnings about attacks and suspicious activity in the wider region. The United States has expanded its naval presence to three aircraft-carrier groups as the confrontation with Iran continues. Iran has threatened shipping and has accused Washington of escalating pressure through a naval blockade. The Gulf remains a vital route for oil and liquefied natural gas exports, meaning disruption can affect freight costs, insurance premiums, energy prices and supply chains well beyond the Middle East. Details about individual incidents, including the identity of attackers and the precise weapons used, should be treated as unconfirmed unless established by maritime authorities. No durable maritime-security agreement has been announced.

africaNews.title: Nigeria's annual inflation eases to 14.06%, but households still face high food costs
africaNews.summary: Nigeria's annual headline inflation eased to 14.06% in October from 14.63% in September. Annual food inflation also slowed to 19.13%, but prices remain high and month-on-month inflation data show that easing annual inflation does not mean the cost of living has fallen.
africaNews.content: Nigeria's annual headline inflation rate eased to 14.06% in October from 14.63% in September, according to data reported by Reuters from the National Bureau of Statistics. Annual food inflation fell to 19.13% from 19.59%. The figures provide evidence that the pace of annual price increases has moderated, but they do not mean that prices have returned to earlier levels. Many households continue to face elevated costs for food, transport, energy and essential services. President Bola Tinubu's administration has defended reforms including the removal of petrol subsidies and currency devaluation as necessary to strengthen public finances and support longer-term growth. Critics point to the immediate burden on consumers and businesses. The political debate ahead of the 2027 election will increasingly focus on whether slower inflation translates into real improvements in purchasing power, employment and household welfare.
